lessons.title: What Is a Signal?
lessons.summary: Sound, pictures and video are all just numbers that change over something.
lessons.demoCaption: Add harmonics to a fundamental and hear the timbre change. Square, sawtooth and triangle waves are just particular harmonic recipes.

blocks.text: A **signal** is any quantity that varies over time or space. The pressure wave hitting a microphone is a signal over time. The brightness of pixels across a photo is a signal over space. A video is both at once: brightness that varies across the frame *and* from frame to frame.

The simplest signal is the **sine wave**. It is described by three numbers: how often it repeats (**frequency**, in hertz), how big it is (**amplitude**), and where in its cycle it starts (**phase**).
x(t) = A · sin(2π f t + φ)
blocks.caption: A = amplitude, f = frequency in Hz, φ = phase in radians

blocks.text: Why care about sines? Because almost any signal can be built by adding sines together. A violin and a flute playing the same note share the same *fundamental* frequency but differ in the mix of *harmonics* — sines at 2×, 3×, 4× the fundamental. That mix is what we hear as **timbre**.
Loudness and pitch are logarithmic

We perceive both pitch and loudness on ratios, not differences. Doubling the frequency raises the pitch one **octave** (A4 = 440 Hz, A5 = 880 Hz). Loudness is measured in **decibels**, a log scale where every 6 dB is roughly a doubling of amplitude.
level (dB) = 20 · log₁₀(A / A_ref)

items: Human hearing spans roughly **20 Hz – 20 kHz**.
In digital audio, 0 dBFS is the loudest possible sample; everything else is negative.
Two identical sines with opposite phase **cancel** — the principle behind noise-cancelling headphones.

blocks.title: On set and in the studio
blocks.body: Flip a mic's polarity and its signal is a sine-by-sine mirror image. Mix it with a second mic on the same source and the low end vanishes — the classic 'phase problem' on a drum kit. Film sound mixers check phase on every multi-mic dialogue scene for the same reason.

quiz.prompt: A tone at 440 Hz is raised by one octave. What is its new frequency?
quiz.explanation: An octave is a doubling of frequency, so 440 Hz → 880 Hz.

quiz.prompt: Two instruments play the same note but sound different. What mainly differs?
quiz.explanation: Same fundamental, different harmonic recipe — that is timbre.

quiz.prompt: Halving a signal's amplitude changes its level by about…

lessons.title: Sampling and Aliasing
lessons.summary: How a continuous wave becomes a list of numbers — and what goes wrong.
lessons.demoCaption: The faint line is the true signal; the dots are the samples. Push the frequency past Nyquist and the samples trace a slower impostor.

blocks.text: A computer can't store a continuous wave. Instead an **analog-to-digital converter** measures it at regular instants — the **sample rate**, *fs*. CD audio takes 44,100 samples per second; film and video sound uses 48,000. A video camera samples the scene too: 24, 30 or 60 times a second.
The Nyquist limit

The **Nyquist–Shannon theorem** says a signal can be reconstructed perfectly from its samples only if it contains no frequencies at or above half the sample rate. That half-rate is the **Nyquist frequency**.
f_Nyquist = fs / 2
blocks.caption: 44.1 kHz audio can represent up to 22.05 kHz — just above human hearing

blocks.text: Frequencies above Nyquist don't disappear — they **fold back** and masquerade as lower ones. This impostor is an **alias**, and once it's in the samples, no processing can tell it apart from a real tone.
f_alias = | f − round(f / fs) · fs |
That is why every converter puts an **anti-aliasing low-pass filter** in front of the sampler, removing content above Nyquist *before* it can fold.

blocks.title: Aliasing you've already seen
blocks.body: The **wagon-wheel effect** — spokes spinning backwards on film — is temporal aliasing at 24 fps. **Moiré** shimmer on a striped shirt is spatial aliasing: the pattern is finer than the sensor's pixel grid, so cameras add an optical low-pass filter. In audio, a cheap synth plug-in that generates a sawtooth naïvely produces aliases that sound like inharmonic whistles on high notes.

quiz.prompt: Audio sampled at 48 kHz can represent frequencies up to…
quiz.explanation: Nyquist frequency = fs / 2 = 24 kHz.

quiz.prompt: A 30 kHz tone is sampled at 44.1 kHz without filtering. What do you hear?
quiz.explanation: It folds back: 44.1 − 30 = 14.1 kHz, squarely audible.

quiz.prompt: Spokes appearing to spin backwards in a film is an example of…
quiz.explanation: The wheel rotates faster than half the frame rate allows, so the sampled motion aliases.

lessons.title: Quantization and Bit Depth
lessons.summary: Every sample must be rounded to a fixed set of levels. The rounding is noise.
lessons.demoCaption: Lower the bit depth and listen: the hiss rises, then turns into a gritty buzz. Turn on dither to hear the buzz turn back into hiss.

blocks.text: Sampling slices *time*. **Quantization** slices *amplitude*: each measured value is rounded to the nearest of 2ᴮ levels, where B is the **bit depth**. The difference between the true value and the rounded value is **quantization error**, and for busy signals it behaves like a quiet hiss.
Dynamic range ≈ 6.02 · B + 1.76 dB
blocks.caption: 16-bit ≈ 98 dB, 24-bit ≈ 146 dB (more than any real microphone can deliver)

blocks.text: Each extra bit halves the step size and buys about 6 dB of headroom. That's why recordings are tracked at 24-bit: you can leave plenty of headroom above the loudest peak and still keep the noise floor far below hearing.
Dither: adding noise to remove distortion

At very low bit depths the error stops being random and starts tracking the signal — it becomes harmonic **distortion**. Adding a tiny amount of random noise before rounding (**dither**) breaks that correlation. You trade an ugly, signal-dependent buzz for a smooth, constant hiss — which our ears forgive far more easily.

blocks.title: Mastering, video banding and HDR
blocks.body: When a 24-bit mix is exported to a 16-bit CD or streaming master, mastering engineers apply dither (often noise-shaped to push the hiss into frequencies we hear least). In pictures, quantization shows up as **banding** in smooth skies on 8-bit video — one of the main reasons HDR and professional grading use 10-bit or more, and why film grain or added noise hides banding so well.

quiz.prompt: How many quantization levels does a 16-bit sample have?
quiz.explanation: 2¹⁶ = 65,536 levels.

quiz.prompt: Roughly how much dynamic range does each extra bit add?
quiz.explanation: Each bit halves the step size: 20·log₁₀(2) ≈ 6 dB.

quiz.prompt: Why add dither before reducing bit depth?
choices: To turn signal-dependent distortion into benign noise
quiz.explanation: Dither decorrelates the error from the signal, replacing distortion with smooth noise.

lessons.title: Fourier and the FFT
lessons.summary: Seeing a signal as a recipe of frequencies.
lessons.demoCaption: Build a signal on the left and watch its spectrum on the right. Each sine you add appears as its own spike.

blocks.text: Lesson 1 built sounds by adding sines. The **Fourier transform** runs that recipe backwards: given a signal, it tells you how much of each frequency it contains. Plotting that is a **spectrum** — the view behind every EQ display and spectrum analyser.
X[k] = Σₙ x[n] · e^(−i 2π k n / N)
blocks.caption: The discrete Fourier transform (DFT) of N samples

blocks.text: Each output **bin** k measures how strongly the signal correlates with a sine at frequency k · fs / N. The bin spacing — the **frequency resolution** — depends only on how many samples you analyse:
Δf = fs / N
blocks.caption: 4,096 samples at 44.1 kHz → bins every 10.8 Hz

blocks.text: Computed directly, the DFT costs N² operations. The **Fast Fourier Transform** (FFT, Cooley–Tukey 1965) gets the same answer in N·log₂N by recursively splitting the problem in half — for N = 4,096 that's about 340× faster. It's the reason real-time spectral audio and video processing exist at all.

items: A pure sine is a single spike. A square wave is spikes at odd harmonics, falling as 1/n.
Noise spreads energy across all bins.
The transform is reversible — you can edit the spectrum and transform back (that's how spectral repair tools work).

blocks.title: Where the FFT runs every day
blocks.body: Spectrum analysers in DAWs, auto-tune's pitch detection, noise-reduction tools that 'learn' a hum profile, MP3/AAC encoders deciding which frequencies you won't miss, and the 'Shazam' style fingerprint that matches songs from a few seconds of spectral peaks.

quiz.prompt: What does the Fourier transform of a signal show?
choices: How much of each frequency it contains
quiz.explanation: It decomposes a signal into its frequency components.

quiz.prompt: With fs = 48 kHz and N = 1,024 samples, what's the bin spacing?
Why is the FFT so important in practice?
choices: It's more accurate than the DFT
It computes the DFT in N·log N instead of N² operations
quiz.explanation: Same result as the DFT, dramatically faster.

lessons.title: Windows and Spectral Leakage
lessons.summary: Why a pure tone doesn't always look like one spike — and how to fix it.
lessons.demoCaption: Slide the tone between bins. On an exact bin it's a clean spike; between bins the rectangular window leaks everywhere. Switch windows to contain it.

blocks.text: The FFT quietly assumes the chunk you hand it repeats forever. If a tone doesn't complete a whole number of cycles in that chunk, the loop has a jump at the seam. That discontinuity smears energy into every bin: **spectral leakage**.

The fix is a **window function** — a smooth fade-in/fade-out applied before the FFT so the chunk's ends meet at zero. Different windows trade **main-lobe width** (how sharp a peak looks) against **side-lobe level** (how far leakage spreads).

items: **Rectangular** (no window): sharpest peak, worst leakage (first side lobe ≈ −13 dB).
**Hann**: the everyday default (≈ −31 dB side lobes).
**Hamming**: lower nearest side lobe (≈ −43 dB), popular in speech.
**Blackman**: very low leakage (≈ −58 dB), wider peak — good for spotting quiet tones next to loud ones.

blocks.title: Choosing a window in real tools
blocks.body: Analyser plug-ins and measurement software like Smaart and REW let you pick the window. Engineers hunting a faint hum under loud music use a low-leakage window; someone tuning two close notes uses one with a narrow main lobe. Every spectrogram, pitch tracker and audio codec makes this choice somewhere.

quiz.prompt: What causes spectral leakage?
choices: Analysing a chunk that doesn't hold a whole number of cycles
quiz.explanation: The implied loop has a discontinuity, spreading energy across bins.

quiz.prompt: Compared with no window, a Hann window gives…
choices: Lower side lobes, slightly wider peak
quiz.explanation: Windowing trades main-lobe width for much lower side lobes.

quiz.prompt: You need to spot a quiet tone right next to a loud one. Which is the best choice?
quiz.explanation: Blackman's very low side lobes stop the loud tone's leakage from burying the quiet one.

lessons.title: Spectrograms and the STFT
lessons.summary: Frequency over time — the picture of sound.
lessons.demoCaption: Pick a test signal and change the window size. Watch the sweep sharpen while the clicks smear — and the other way round.

blocks.text: A single FFT tells you *what* frequencies are present but not *when*. The **short-time Fourier transform** (STFT) slides a window along the signal, takes an FFT at each step, and stacks the results side by side. Plotted with time across, frequency up and brightness for level, that's a **spectrogram**.
Time resolution ≈ N / fs     Frequency resolution ≈ fs / N
blocks.caption: You can't have both — a longer window sharpens frequency and blurs time

blocks.text: This **time–frequency trade-off** is fundamental (it's the signal-processing cousin of the uncertainty principle). Short windows show crisp drum hits but blurry pitches; long windows show clean harmonics but smeared attacks. Overlapping frames (a **hop** smaller than the window) make the picture smoother.

blocks.title: Reading sound like a picture
blocks.body: Dialogue editors use spectral editors such as iZotope RX to paint out a cough, a phone ring or a chair creak that sits between words. Bird researchers identify species by spectrogram shape. Speech recognisers, including the one in your phone, start from a (mel-scaled) spectrogram.

quiz.prompt: What are a spectrogram's axes?
choices: Frequency vs. time, with color for level
quiz.explanation: Time across, frequency up, brightness or color for level.

quiz.prompt: You lengthen the STFT window. What happens?
choices: Better frequency resolution, worse time resolution
Better time resolution, worse frequency resolution
quiz.explanation: More samples per FFT → finer bins but each column covers more time.

quiz.prompt: A dialogue editor removes a phone ring between words without touching the voice. Which tool are they most likely using?
quiz.explanation: Spectral editing lets you select and attenuate a region of time AND frequency.

lessons.title: Convolution and Impulse Responses
lessons.summary: One operation behind blur, echo, reverb and every linear filter.
lessons.demoCaption: Choose a kernel (impulse response) and see what convolution does to a noisy signal. The echo kernel is easiest to hear.

blocks.text: Clap in a cathedral and you hear the clap followed by a long, decaying wash. That wash is the room's **impulse response** — its reaction to a single instantaneous click. For any **linear, time-invariant** system (a room, a speaker, an EQ, a lens blur), the impulse response tells you *everything*: the output for any input is the input **convolved** with it.
y[n] = Σₖ h[k] · x[n − k]
blocks.caption: Each output sample is a weighted sum of recent inputs, weights = impulse response h

blocks.text: Read it as: *drop a scaled copy of h at every input sample and add them all up*. A short h of equal weights is a **moving average** that smooths noise. An h with a spike at a delay is an **echo**. An h recorded in a real hall is that hall's **reverb**.
The convolution theorem

Convolution in time equals multiplication in frequency. So a filter's spectrum (its **frequency response**) is simply the FFT of its impulse response — and long convolutions are computed fastest by FFT-multiply-inverse-FFT.
y = x ∗ h   ⇔   Y(f) = X(f) · H(f)

blocks.title: Convolution in production
blocks.body: Convolution reverbs (Altiverb, Logic's Space Designer) load impulse responses recorded in real churches, studios and car interiors — post-production uses them to make ADR dialogue sound like it was recorded on location. Guitar cab simulators are convolution with a speaker IR. In images, every blur, sharpen and edge filter is a 2-D convolution (Lesson 10).

quiz.prompt: What is an impulse response?
choices: A system's output for a single click input
The loudest sample in a file
quiz.explanation: It's the system's reaction to an ideal impulse — and it fully characterises an LTI system.

quiz.prompt: Convolving with a longer moving-average kernel makes the signal…
quiz.explanation: Averaging more samples is a stronger low-pass filter.

quiz.prompt: Convolution in the time domain corresponds to what in the frequency domain?
quiz.explanation: The convolution theorem: Y(f) = X(f)·H(f).

lessons.title: FIR and IIR Filters and EQ
lessons.summary: Shaping the spectrum: low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, peaking EQ.
lessons.demoCaption: Design a biquad and see its frequency response. Then run it on noise or a sawtooth and listen.

blocks.text: A **filter** changes the balance of frequencies. There are two families:

items: **FIR** (finite impulse response): output = weighted sum of inputs only. Always stable, can have perfectly linear phase, but needs many taps for steep slopes.
**IIR** (infinite impulse response): output also feeds back past *outputs*. Very efficient — a few multiplies give a steep filter — but phase is non-linear and poor design can go unstable.

blocks.text: The workhorse of audio is the **biquad**, a 2nd-order IIR with two zeros and two poles. Every parametric EQ band in your DAW is a biquad, typically from Robert Bristow-Johnson's *Audio EQ Cookbook*.
y[n] = b₀x[n] + b₁x[n−1] + b₂x[n−2] − a₁y[n−1] − a₂y[n−2]

The controls map onto the maths: **cutoff/centre frequency** sets where the filter acts, **Q** sets how narrow the region is (and how resonant the corner), **gain** sets how much a peaking band boosts or cuts.

blocks.title: Filters everywhere
blocks.body: A high-pass at 80 Hz on dialogue removes traffic rumble and handling noise. A notch at 50/60 Hz kills mains hum. A low-pass is the anti-aliasing filter in every converter. Synthesizers sweep a resonant low-pass for the classic 'wah'. Crossovers in speakers split bands to woofer and tweeter. Camera sensors carry an optical low-pass filter for the same anti-aliasing job.

quiz.prompt: Which filter removes low-frequency rumble from dialogue?
quiz.explanation: A high-pass passes highs and removes lows.

quiz.prompt: What distinguishes an IIR filter from an FIR filter?
choices: IIR uses feedback of past outputs
quiz.explanation: The feedback terms (a₁, a₂) make the impulse response ring on forever.

quiz.prompt: Raising a peaking EQ band's Q does what?
quiz.explanation: Q is centre frequency ÷ bandwidth; higher Q = narrower band.

lessons.title: Dynamics: Compressors and Limiters
lessons.summary: Turning the volume knob automatically, thousands of times a second.
lessons.demoCaption: A drum loop with loud and quiet hits. Lower the threshold and raise the ratio to even them out; listen before and after.

blocks.text: Filters change *frequency* balance. **Dynamics processors** change *level* over time. A **compressor** watches the signal's level and turns it down when it rises above a **threshold**, by an amount set by the **ratio**.
out = T + (in − T) / R     (when in > T, all in dB)
blocks.caption: Ratio 4:1 → 4 dB over the threshold comes out as 1 dB over

items: **Attack** — how quickly gain reduction kicks in. Slow attack lets transients (the 'snap' of a drum) through.
**Release** — how quickly it recovers once the level falls.
**Make-up gain** — raises the whole result back up, so the quiet parts end up louder than before.
A **limiter** is a compressor with a very high ratio and fast attack: a ceiling nothing crosses.

blocks.text: Under the hood it's an **envelope follower** (a one-pole low-pass on the rectified signal, with different coefficients for attack and release) driving a gain computer. Note it's *non-linear* — it can't be described by an impulse response.

blocks.title: Why everything you hear is compressed
blocks.body: Broadcast and streaming platforms normalise to a loudness target (measured in LUFS — often around −14 LUFS for music streaming and −23/−24 LUFS for broadcast TV), so mixes are compressed to sit consistently. Film mixers ride dialogue with compression so whispers survive a noisy cinema, and a **limiter** on the master protects against overs. A **de-esser** is a compressor that only listens to the 'sss' band; **sidechain** compression ducks music under a voice-over.

quiz.prompt: With a −20 dB threshold and 4:1 ratio, an input at −8 dB comes out at…
quiz.explanation: 12 dB over threshold ÷ 4 = 3 dB over → −17 dB.

quiz.prompt: A slow attack time lets what through?
quiz.explanation: The gain reduction lags behind, so the first few ms of a hit pass untouched.

quiz.prompt: Why is a compressor not described by an impulse response?
choices: It's non-linear — its gain depends on the input level
quiz.explanation: Impulse responses characterise linear systems; a compressor's behaviour changes with level.

lessons.title: Images as 2-D Signals
lessons.summary: Blur, sharpen and edge detection are convolution in two dimensions.
lessons.demoCaption: Apply kernels to a test card (or your own photo). Look at the fine stripes and text — that's where the high frequencies live.

blocks.text: An image is a signal over *space*: brightness as a function of (x, y). Everything from Module 3 carries over. **Spatial frequency** measures how fast brightness changes across the frame — smooth skies are low frequency, fine fabric, hair and text are high frequency.
2-D filters are small grids of weights called **kernels**. Each output pixel is the weighted sum of its neighbourhood:
y[i, j] = Σₘ Σₙ h[m, n] · x[i − m, j − n]

items: **Box / Gaussian blur** — low-pass filters. A Gaussian looks natural because it has no hard edges of its own.
**Sharpen** — boosts the centre and subtracts the neighbours: a high-frequency boost (an 'unsharp mask' is original + amount × (original − blur)).
**Sobel** — approximates the brightness gradient; large values mark **edges**, the first step of Canny edge detection and many computer-vision pipelines.

blocks.title: In cameras, grading suites and VFX
blocks.body: Every camera runs sharpening and noise reduction (low-pass filtering) in its image pipeline. Colourists use blur for skin softening and unsharp-mask for detail. Compositors use edge detection for mattes and to drive rotoscoping; depth-of-field and bokeh effects are convolution with a disc-shaped kernel. Downscaling 4K to HD without a low-pass first creates moiré — 2-D aliasing.

quiz.prompt: A Gaussian blur is which kind of filter?
quiz.explanation: It averages neighbours, removing fine (high-frequency) detail.

quiz.prompt: What does a Sobel kernel detect?
quiz.explanation: Sobel approximates the derivative of brightness, which is large at edges.

quiz.prompt: Which image content has the highest spatial frequencies?
quiz.explanation: Rapid changes in brightness over short distances = high spatial frequency.

lessons.title: The DCT and How JPEG and Video Compress
lessons.summary: Throw away the frequencies nobody will miss.
lessons.demoCaption: Lower the quality and watch blocks and ringing appear — and the share of coefficients that became zero (free to compress) climb.

blocks.text: Uncompressed 4K video at 24 fps is over 4 Gbit/s. Streaming services send roughly a hundredth of that. The trick is the **discrete cosine transform** (DCT), a Fourier cousin that turns each small block of pixels into a grid of spatial-frequency coefficients.
F[u, v] = ¼ C(u)C(v) Σₓ Σᵧ f[x, y] cos((2x+1)uπ/16) cos((2y+1)vπ/16)
blocks.caption: JPEG's 8×8 DCT-II; u, v = horizontal and vertical frequency

blocks.text: For natural images, almost all the energy lands in a few low-frequency coefficients. JPEG then **quantizes** each coefficient — dividing by a table that's coarse for high frequencies (where the eye is least sensitive) — and most high-frequency values round to **zero**. Long runs of zeros compress beautifully with entropy coding.

items: Quantization is where information is lost — the DCT itself is perfectly reversible.
Too-aggressive quantization shows as **blocking** (visible 8×8 squares) and **ringing** near sharp edges.
Color is usually stored at lower resolution than brightness (**chroma subsampling**, e.g. 4:2:0), because we see detail mainly in luminance.

blocks.title: From JPEG to H.264, HEVC and ProRes
blocks.body: Video codecs reuse this idea per frame and add **motion compensation**: predict each block from a previous frame, then DCT-code only the error. H.264 uses 4×4 and 8×8 integer transforms, HEVC up to 32×32. ProRes and DNxHR, the editing codecs, are intra-frame DCT codecs that keep every frame independent for easy scrubbing. Audio codecs (MP3, AAC) use the MDCT, a close relative.

quiz.prompt: In JPEG, where is information actually lost?
quiz.explanation: The DCT and entropy coding are lossless; rounding coefficients is not.

quiz.prompt: Why does JPEG quantize high-frequency coefficients more coarsely?
choices: The eye is less sensitive to fine detail errors
quiz.explanation: Perceptual weighting: spend bits where the eye notices.

quiz.prompt: What extra trick do video codecs add on top of per-block DCT coding?
quiz.explanation: Most of a frame is predictable from its neighbours; only the residual is coded.

lessons.title: Frame Rates, Shutter and Motion
lessons.summary: Film is sampling in time — and the shutter is its anti-aliasing filter.
lessons.demoCaption: A spinning wheel filmed at the frame rate and shutter angle you choose. Find speeds where it freezes or turns backwards, then widen the shutter.

blocks.text: A movie camera samples the world in time: **24 frames per second** for cinema, 25 for PAL regions, 30/60 for much of TV and online video. Everything from Lesson 2 applies — fast periodic motion above half the frame rate **aliases**.

The **shutter** decides how long each frame is exposed. Cinematographers describe it as a **shutter angle**, from the spinning-disc shutters of film cameras: 360° means the shutter is open for the whole frame interval.
exposure time = (shutter angle / 360°) × (1 / fps)
blocks.caption: The cinema standard: 180° at 24 fps → 1/48 s

blocks.text: Exposing over an interval *averages* motion — a box filter in time. That **motion blur** is a temporal low-pass filter: it softens the strobing and aliasing that a pure instantaneous sample would produce. Too little (a 45° shutter, as in the battle in *Saving Private Ryan*) gives a jittery, staccato look; too much smears everything.
Flicker and frame-rate conversion

items: Mains-powered lights flicker at 100 or 120 Hz. Shoot with the wrong shutter speed and that aliases into slow visible pulsing — why crews in 50 Hz countries shoot at 1/50 s or 1/100 s.
Converting 24 fps to 60 Hz TV uses **3:2 pulldown** (alternately showing frames 3 and 2 fields long), which adds judder.
Motion-interpolation ('smooth motion' on TVs) estimates in-between frames — the 'soap-opera effect' many filmmakers dislike.

blocks.title: Decisions on a real shoot
blocks.body: A DP shooting a car commercial watches the wheels: at certain speeds they freeze or spin backwards, so they adjust speed, frame rate or add blur in post. Shooting a computer monitor or LED wall, they sync shutter to the screen's refresh. Slow-motion at 120 fps needs short shutters and lots of light, because the exposure per frame shrinks.

quiz.prompt: At 24 fps with a 180° shutter, what's the exposure time?
Motion blur acts like what kind of filter?
quiz.explanation: Averaging over the exposure interval removes fast temporal changes.

quiz.prompt: A wheel with 8 identical spokes spins at exactly 3 revolutions per second, filmed at 24 fps. What does it look like?
quiz.explanation: Each frame it turns 3/24 = 1/8 revolution — exactly one spoke spacing — so every frame looks identical.

lessons.title: Colour, Gamma and Chroma
lessons.summary: Why pixel values aren't light, how cameras neutralise the colour of the light, and why colour can be stored at lower resolution than brightness.
lessons.demoCaption: Three parts. Gamma: lower the bit depth and compare where linear storage bands. Chroma: subsample the colour and look at the red text on blue. White balance: light the chart with tungsten, then fix it with the camera setting, Auto, or a click on a gray patch.

blocks.text: A camera sensor counts photons, so its raw output is proportional to **linear light**: twice the photons, twice the value. Our eyes don't work that way. We're far more sensitive to small changes in dark tones than in bright ones, and perceived lightness grows roughly with the cube root of light.

**Gamma encoding** bridges the two. Before storing a pixel, the camera raises linear light to a power of about 1/2.2 (the *transfer function*), so equal steps in code value look like equal steps in brightness. The display applies the inverse power to turn codes back into light.
V = L^(1/γ)      L = V^γ
blocks.caption: L = linear light, V = stored value, both 0…1. γ ≈ 2.2 for sRGB; HD/TV mastering displays use 2.4 (BT.1886)

blocks.text: It matters because every value is **quantized** (Lesson 3). Store 8-bit values linearly and the darkest 10% of light gets only about 26 codes, so shadows band visibly, while the highlights get codes the eye can't tell apart. With sRGB encoding, the same 10% gets about 90 codes.
Colour as three signals

Screens mix red, green and blue light. Video and JPEG convert gamma-encoded R′G′B′ into **Y′** (luma, the brightness signal) and two **colour-difference** signals: Cb (blue minus luma) and Cr (red minus luma).

blocks.caption: BT.601 weights, used by JPEG; HD video (BT.709) uses 0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722

blocks.text: The eye resolves fine detail in brightness much better than in colour, so the colour-difference signals can be stored at lower resolution. That's **chroma subsampling**. 4:2:2 halves chroma horizontally. 4:2:0 halves it both ways, keeping a quarter of the chroma samples and half the total data of 4:4:4.

items: **4:4:4**: full colour resolution. Used for VFX plates, computer graphics and screen recordings.
**4:2:2**: broadcast and mastering formats such as ProRes 422 and XAVC.
**4:2:0**: almost all delivery. Streaming, Blu-ray, H.264/HEVC, phone video and most JPEGs.

blocks.text: White balance

Light itself has a colour. A candle or tungsten bulb is orange (2,000–3,200 K), noon daylight is near neutral (about 5,600 K) and open shade is blue (7,000 K and above). The numbers are **colour temperatures**: the temperature of a glowing black body that emits light of that colour.

A sensor just records reflectance × light, so a white shirt under tungsten records as orange. Our brains discount the light automatically; cameras do it with **white balance**: one gain per channel, applied in linear light, chosen so a neutral object comes out with R = G = B.
R_out = R_in · g_R     G_out = G_in · 1     B_out = B_in · g_B
blocks.caption: Gains are relative to green. Setting the camera to the light's temperature picks gains that cancel it.

items: **Presets** (tungsten, daylight, shade) set the gains for a known light.
**Auto white balance** guesses the light from the image. The simplest method, *gray world*, assumes the scene averages to gray, which fails when one colour dominates (a sunset, a green forest).
**Custom white balance**: shoot or click a known neutral, like a gray card, and use its colour as the light.

blocks.title: Grading, keying and delivery
blocks.body: Camera crews white-balance on a **gray card** at the start of each setup, and mixed lighting (a tungsten lamp in a daylit room) is corrected with gels on the lights because one white balance can't fix both. Colourists do maths like exposure and blending in **linear light**, where it's physically correct, then encode for the display. Camera **log** curves (S-Log, LogC, V-Log) are extreme transfer functions that fit 14+ stops of dynamic range into 10 bits. Green-screen keys pull far cleaner edges from 4:4:4 or 4:2:2 footage than 4:2:0, because the edge lives in the chroma. Designers avoid thin, saturated red text over blue in delivered video, because 4:2:0 smears it. HDR replaces gamma with the PQ (SMPTE ST 2084) and HLG transfer functions.

quiz.prompt: Why do images and video store gamma-encoded values instead of linear light?
choices: To spend code values evenly in perceived brightness, so shadows don't band
quiz.explanation: Quantization steps are spread where the eye is most sensitive: the dark tones.

quiz.prompt: What does 4:2:0 chroma subsampling reduce?
choices: Colour resolution, both horizontally and vertically
quiz.explanation: Chroma is stored at half resolution in both directions; luma stays at full resolution.

quiz.prompt: Why does chroma subsampling usually go unnoticed?
choices: The eye sees fine detail mainly in brightness, not colour
quiz.explanation: Our visual system resolves luminance detail much better than chrominance detail, so halving chroma resolution is hard to see in most images.

quiz.prompt: A scene lit by tungsten bulbs (3,200 K) is shot with the camera set to daylight (5,600 K). How does it look?
quiz.explanation: The daylight setting doesn't cancel the extra red of tungsten light, so everything comes out orange. Setting the camera to 3,200 K fixes it.
